title: Design a Low-Latency Listing Search System
prompt:
Design a search service for millions of accommodation listings. Guests submit location and price filters and receive low-latency, relevance-ranked results with pagination. Host edits and listing removals must become visible within a freshness target you define.

Clarify query and price semantics, then describe the API, data model, indexing, updates, and serving path. State scale and latency assumptions and discuss popular-location hotspots and partial failures. Booking, payment, and authoritative stay availability are outside this exercise.

response.placeholder: Clarify location and price semantics, then trace one search and one listing update. State how ranking, pagination, and failure behavior preserve your contract.
response.reference_answer:
## 1. Contract and capacity

I would confirm that the initial product is discovery using indicative nightly prices. Date-specific totals and bookable availability need additional pricing/calendar services and a different latency budget. Search results include the price basis, currency, and a freshness indicator so guests do not confuse discovery with a guaranteed quote.

For the assumed workload, 10 million documents at an illustrative 2 KB each give 20 GB of raw searchable fields. Index structures, replicas, and rebuild headroom multiply that; I would measure actual index expansion before selecting machines. At peak, 10,000 requests/s with an average four-shard fan-out means roughly 40,000 shard searches/s before retries. This is a planning assumption to validate with real query geography, filter selectivity, and cache hit rates. Photos belong in object storage/CDN, not search documents.

An initial 200 ms deadline might reserve 15 ms for admission and routing, 70 ms for parallel retrieval, 40 ms for reranking, 35 ms for batched hydration/filter rechecks, and 40 ms of headroom. These are stage deadlines, not a claim that adding stage p95s proves an end-to-end p95. Load tests must measure the full distribution, especially broad map queries and hot destinations.

## 2. API and data ownership

`POST /search` accepts a location shape, optional text, inclusive price bounds, currency, order, page size, and optional opaque cursor. It returns listing summaries, indicative prices, a next cursor, freshness metadata, and an explicit partial-results indicator when applicable. Reject invalid coordinates, negative or reversed price ranges, excessive page sizes, and overly broad unsupported regions with a clear error. A bounding box crossing the antimeridian is split into two longitude ranges.

A durable listing database owns listing ID, host ID, status, searchable coordinates, title, amenities, base price/currency, and a monotonically increasing listing version. Search documents are projections containing geo fields, tokenized text, numeric prices, status, quality features, and that version. Host writes commit an outbox event with the database mutation; search is never a synchronous participant in that transaction.

Use integer monetary units and one pinned exchange-rate version per search session. Convert filter bounds with explicit ceil/floor rules to avoid silently dropping boundary prices, and recheck the displayed converted price against the original bounds. The same price representation and rounding define ascending price order. A rate-table change invalidates affected cached results or creates a new cache namespace.

## 3. Retrieval and geographic partitioning

The query service canonicalizes the query and routes it through a geographic partition directory. Each partition has replicas and indexes for geo intersection, numeric ranges, and text retrieval. Geography limits fan-out for ordinary destination searches, but dense cities need subdivisions or secondary hash partitions; one city must not be forced onto a single shard. The router covers every cell intersecting the query shape and deduplicates any replicated boundary documents by listing ID.

Geo cells are candidate routing aids. Apply the exact bounding-box or distance predicate and price/status filters inside retrieval; a cell intersection alone is not a match. Return no matches when filters exclude everything, rather than silently expanding the region or budget. The directory and index generation must agree during partition changes; dual reads or an atomic generation switch avoid gaps.

Begin with a transparent relevance score using text match, distance, listing quality, and suitable product signals. Normalize features consistently across shards. Price sorting uses a globally comparable `(converted_price, listing_id)` key. For a shared deterministic score, each shard's local top-k contains enough candidates to compute the global top-k after merging. If a later reranker changes the score, local top-k under the retrieval score does not guarantee the true global optimum: overfetch, measure candidate recall, and explicitly accept approximation. Diversity constraints also require extra candidates.

## 4. Ranking, caching, and pagination

Merge candidates, batch-fetch ranking features, rerank a bounded set, and hydrate listing cards in bulk. Recheck current status and the selected displayed price before returning a card. If an updated listing no longer qualifies, skip it and consume more candidates within the deadline; a short page is preferable to a filter violation. Price edits can still race after this check, so the result remains advisory.

Cache shared candidate sets for canonical query/region/filter combinations. Include ordering, currency/rate version, index generation, and any personalization cohort in cache keys. TTLs and event-driven invalidation bound staleness; single-flight refresh and TTL jitter prevent a cache stampede. A cached result still passes the status/price serving checks. Cache broad regional candidates only if every request reapplies its exact filters.

For an initial implementation, materialize a short-lived ordered list of up to 500 result IDs with pinned displayed prices and ranking version. A signed cursor identifies the session and next candidate offset, binding the normalized query and order. Consume each candidate position at most once across sequential pages; retries with the same cursor reproduce the same page when still valid. Save each emitted page for retry consistency, subject to removal suppression. Expire the session after an assumed five minutes and ask the client to restart for deeper exploration. If a current price differs from the pinned session price, omit that listing rather than insert it at a new position; this preserves the relative order of retained results. Deletions can shorten pages, and retry pages may lose removed items.

The memory cost is explicit: 2,000 new sessions/s times 300 seconds times 500 IDs times 8 bytes is 2.4 GB for IDs alone; price, metadata, and replication add substantially more. Admit fewer sessions, shorten TTLs, or use search-engine point-in-time snapshots plus `search_after` if measurements favor that trade-off. An offset against a continuously changing live ranking does not satisfy the no-duplicate contract.

## 5. Updates, removals, and recovery

A host price edit commits listing version v and an outbox record. At-least-once consumers apply it only if v exceeds the indexed version; an older retry cannot overwrite a newer price. Keep deletion tombstones with versions so a delayed upsert cannot resurrect a removed listing. Dead-letter handling, replay, and reconciliation repair missed events. Rebuild a new index from a consistent snapshot plus the change stream, verify catch-up, then switch the routing alias.

A removal also updates a serving suppression store checked during hydration, including cached/session results. Its propagation delay is a separate measured bound; asynchronous suppression alone is not an instantaneous deletion guarantee. If the product requires immediate removal, require an authoritative status check or acknowledgment from the serving gate before reporting the removal effective. When that required check is unavailable, omit affected cards or fail the request instead of promising that stale cached status is safe.

## 6. Failure behavior and validation

A popular city gets extra replicas, split partitions, cache warming, and admission control. Limit fan-out and expensive query complexity. One bounded retry to a healthy replica may help a slow shard; unbounded retries amplify overload. If a shard misses the deadline, either return an explicitly incomplete response or fail when complete price ordering is required. Do not issue a normal complete-session cursor over silently missing shards.

If learned reranking is unavailable, use the retrieval score with a labeled ranking version. Filters remain mandatory. A lagging index can serve within the declared freshness policy, with lag surfaced; beyond that policy, degrade explicitly or reject requests requiring fresher data. Availability targets do not justify claiming fresh or complete results without evidence.

Measure end-to-end p50/p95/p99, shard tail latency, fan-out, cache hit rate, hydration drops, partial/error rates, session memory, and outbox-to-index lag. Evaluate relevance with judged-query metrics such as NDCG and candidate recall; use guarded online experiments for search engagement and downstream successful bookings. Validate price/geo boundaries, antimeridian queries, empty results, duplicate-free paging during edits, event replay, tombstone resurrection, and shard/ranker outages.

The central trade-off is low-latency discovery against freshness and complete ranking. A derived search index and bounded candidate reranking make discovery fast, while explicit consistency limits and serving checks keep that speed from becoming an unsupported booking or price guarantee.
